title: How can we find out about the past?
essentialQuestion: How do we know what happened before we were born?
learningGoal: Use two sources to make a claim about the past and explain what the sources cannot tell us.

warmUp.question: Look at the three sources about Riverstone Market. What is one thing you notice?

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: What does each source show? What does it leave out?

sources.caption: Source 1: A drawing of Riverstone Market, about 70 years ago
Source 2: A receipt from a Riverstone food shop
Source 3: A diary entry by a young person who lived in Riverstone
details: "Market day was crowded today. My mother sold two baskets of vegetables. Traders arrived by boat before sunrise. I helped carry the vegetables to our stall."

sections.heading: Sources are clues about the past
sections.text: Nobody alive today saw the world as it was 1,000 years ago, so how do we know about it? A historian is a person who studies the past by looking for sources. A source is anything that gives us information about the past. Letters, photographs, drawings, tools, receipts, buildings and maps can all be sources, and so can memories that older people share. Each source is like a clue in a puzzle. The Riverstone drawing, receipt and diary are three sources about one market. A historian uses clues like these as evidence and then makes a claim about what happened.
sections.simpler: Nobody today saw the world long ago. So how do we learn about it? A historian is a person who studies the past. Historians look at sources. A source tells us something about the past. It can be a letter, a photo or a tool. It can be a story that an older person tells. Each source is a clue. We use clues as evidence. Evidence helps us make a claim about the past.

sections.heading: Each source answers different questions
sections.text: Different sources can answer different questions about the past. The receipt shows what one shop sold and the price of each item, so it tells us that rice cost 12 tokens. The drawing shows what the market looked like, with stalls, baskets and a cart. However, the artist may have left some details out. The diary describes what one young person saw and did on market day. It says that traders arrived by boat before sunrise, but one person cannot see everything. So a historian always asks two questions: What does this source tell me, and what can it not tell me?
sections.simpler: Each source answers different questions. The receipt shows prices. Rice cost 12 tokens. The drawing shows what the market looked like. But the artist may leave things out. The diary tells what one young person saw. It says traders came by boat. But one person cannot see everything. So ask two questions. What does this source tell me? What does it not tell me?

sections.heading: Historians compare sources
sections.text: One source almost never tells the whole story, so historians compare sources. To compare means to look at two things and notice how they are similar or different. The drawing shows a river, and the diary says that traders came by boat. Together, these clues suggest that the river helped people bring goods to the market. A historian also asks who made each source, and why they made it. Some questions stay open, because none of the sources tells us how many people lived in Riverstone. A strong claim explains what the evidence shows and what we still do not know.
sections.simpler: One source does not tell the whole story. So historians compare sources. They look for what is the same and what is different. The drawing shows a river. The diary talks about boats. So the river may have helped traders get to the market. Some things we still do not know. No source says how many people lived there. A good claim says what we know. It also says what we do not know.

glossary.definition: A person who studies the past.
glossary.example: A historian might read old letters to learn how people lived.

glossary.definition: Anything that gives us information about the past.
glossary.example: The Riverstone receipt is a source about prices.

glossary.definition: Information that helps show something is true.
glossary.example: The receipt is evidence that the shop sold rice.

glossary.definition: An idea you say is true and back up with reasons.
glossary.example: My claim is that Riverstone Market was busy.

glossary.definition: To look at two things to see how they are alike or different.
glossary.example: We compare the drawing and the diary to learn more about the market.

checks.question: Which source is best for finding the price of rice?

options.feedback: Not quite. The drawing shows what the market looked like, but it has no prices. Look for the source that lists prices.
Not quite. The diary tells what one person saw and did. It does not list prices. Look for the source that lists prices.
Yes. A receipt lists what someone bought and how much it cost. It shows that rice cost 12 tokens.

checks.question: Why do historians compare more than one source?

options.text: One source rarely tells the whole story
options.feedback: Yes. Each source shows only part of the past. When you compare sources, you get a fuller picture.

options.text: Old sources are almost always wrong
options.feedback: Not quite. Old sources are not always wrong. Each one shows a part of the story. Look again at the section about comparing sources.

options.text: Every source gives exactly the same facts
options.feedback: Not quite. Sources often give different facts. That is why historians compare them. Look again at the section about comparing sources.

checks.question: What is one thing about Riverstone that the sources do not tell us?

write.prompt: Make one claim about Riverstone Market. Use evidence from two sources, then name one thing the sources cannot tell us.
sentenceStarters: The receipt or the diary also shows ...
But the sources do not tell us ...
selfCheck: I made one claim about the market.
I used evidence from two sources.
I named one thing the sources cannot tell us.
write.example: I think Riverstone Market was a busy place where people traded food. The drawing shows stalls selling food and cloth. It also shows people carrying baskets. The diary also shows that the market was crowded. It says traders came by boat before sunrise. Together, these sources suggest that the river helped traders bring goods to the market. But the sources do not tell us how many people lived in Riverstone. They also do not tell us what the market was like on other days.

speak.partnerTask: Tell a partner your claim about Riverstone Market. Your partner asks, "Which evidence supports your claim?" Then switch.
speak.independentTask: Say your claim out loud. Name the two sources you used and one thing you still do not know.

watch.title: What is a primary source? (2/3)
watch.why: It explains primary sources, which is what the Riverstone drawing, receipt and diary are.
watch.beforeQuestion: Could an everyday receipt help someone learn about the past?
watch.afterQuestion: What question could the Riverstone receipt answer? What question could it not answer?
watch.summary: This short video explains primary sources. A primary source was made at the time you are studying, often by someone who was there. Letters, diaries, photos, receipts, maps and tools can all be primary sources. They do not have to be famous or special. An everyday receipt can show what people bought and what it cost. A diary can show what one person saw and felt. But each primary source shows only part of the story. So historians ask who made it, when, and why. Then they compare it with other sources. In this lesson, the drawing, the receipt and the diary are all primary sources. Together, they tell us more than any one of them alone.
keyPoints: A primary source was made at the time you are studying.
Everyday things, like receipts, can be useful sources.
Historians compare sources because one source rarely tells the whole story.

educatorNotes: Riverstone and its three sources are fictional. If you can, add one real local source, such as an old photo of a market, and ask the same two questions: what does it tell us, and what can it not tell us?
Riverstone comes back in Lessons 3, 8, 9 and 11. Keep the three sources on screen while learners write.
The video uses fairly fast English. Learners can read the written summary instead; it covers the main idea.
